newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW-Lockheed eyes European aircraft deals.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Lockheed eyes European aircraft deals.

text.p: U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin is in talks with partner firms in Europe's Airbus consortium over designing and building a large military aircraft, a senior Lockheed executive told Reuters on Saturday.
Lockheed Martin is a company with sales of $27 billion a year forged out of a succession of rapid mergers, with interests spanning combat planes, rockets, satellites and high-tech operations.
It is looking to diversify into international markets by partnering with foreign companies.

An Airbus Industrie project to build an in-flight refuelling tanker was one of the planes the U.S. company has been discussing, James Blackwell, president and chief operating officer at Lockheed Martin's aeronautics sector told Reuters at the Paris airshow.
"That's one of the projects we have talked about," he said.
But Airbus has not taken a firm decision to go ahead with the project, he said. The tanker plane would meet the U.S. government's need for a replacement for the KC-135 aircraft.

A related area of possible co-operation was a replacement plane for the U.S. strategic military transporter C141, Lockheed Martin spokesman Lee Whitney said. The U.S. company has been talking to both Airbus and Aerospatiale, the French partner in the consortium, as well as the other partners, he said.
There were no deadlines for the talks and no decisions have been made, he said.

Lockheed Martin is also interested in bidding to supply engine parts -- thrust reversers and nacelles -- to two key Airbus derivatives planned for its A340 long-range airliners, the A340-500 and 600, Blackwell said.

But Airbus has not yet chosen the engines for the new A340 models, which are planned as its stop-gap product against archrival Boeing's 747 jumbo jet, until it launches its high-capacity jet, the A3XX, which would seat 500 passengers.
Pratt & Whitney, a unit of United Technologies Corp, and Rolls Royce Plc are bidding to supply motors to Airbus on the A340-500 and 600.
"If it was a single engine deal, we would be interested," Blackwell said, referring to a potential exclusive engine supply agreement between one of the motor companies and Airbus.

Lockheed Martin is also keen to make aerostructure parts for the A3XX, which is under urgent study by Airbus, but Blackwell ruled out for the time being becoming a risk-sharing partner in the project, whose development costs are expected to be at least $8 billion. "I'm not interested in buying shares," he said.
Lockheed Martin is happy to be a subcontractor in commercial aircraft selling aircraft parts to both Airbus and Boeing, rather than seeking a role as a prime contractor, he said.

Since the U.S. firm saw in 1987 that the Pentagon's spending would fall, Lockheed Martin has aimed for global markets. The aeronautics sector expects to make more than half its sales from international contracts in the next five years. Its 1996 sales were "less than $6 billion," Blackwell said.

However, it harbours big ambitions in military aircraft, where it holds a prime contractor role with Boeing on the U.S. government's new F22 plane and is competing in a two-way race against Boeing on the futuristic Joint Strike Fighter (JSF).

Industry analysts have questioned whether Washington will have money for both costly fighter programmes, but Blackwell was confident the two planes would be funded. "I think there will be funds for both."

Blackwell hoped British Aerospace Plc (BAe) would join the Lockheed Martin JSF team, as the U.K. company has "substantial experience in STOL" (Short Take-Off and Landing) and "is a premier fighter house".
The British navy is looking to buy the JSF as replacement for its carrier-borne Sea Harrier and has put up 200 million pounds towards the development of the two competing prototypes.
Separately, BAe joint managing director John Weston told Reuters that British Aerospace would pick which JSF team it would join shortly, but no decision had been made yet.
Its workshare is a key issue with BAe seeing a potential 10 percent of the $90 billion JSF contract for the Pentagon.
